newsitem.title: KUWAIT: French team removes 10 bullets from Uday - report.
newsitem.headline: French team removes 10 bullets from Uday - report.

text.p: An Iraqi opposition group said in remarks published on Saturday that a French medical team had removed 10 bullets from Iraqi leader Saddam Hussein's son Uday but had refused to operate on a bullet still in his spine.

Uday, 32, was shot in an assassination attempt while driving through Baghdad on December 12. He told a visiting Palestinian cleric from his hospital bed early this month that four bullets were still lodged in his body.

"A French medical team has refused to conduct surgery to remove a bullet that settled in Uday's spine," Bayan Jabr, a member of the opposition Supreme Council for the Islamic Revolution in Iraq (SCIRI), was quoted as saying by Kuwait's al-Rai al-Aam newspaper.
The team did not explain the reason for declining to operate on Uday but Iraqi doctors said such surgery involved high risk, Jabr added.

Jabr, a representative in Damascus for SCIRI, a Shi'ite Moslem group with a Tehran-based leader, said the French medical team had removed 10 bullets from Uday and that he had the beginnings of gangrene in his left leg which might require amputation of the infected part.
Uday and other senior Iraqi officials have blamed Iran for the attack which occurred in a wealthy Baghdad suburb.
Saddam's eldest son -- said by some opposition elements to be Iraq's second most powerful figure after his father -- has been shown on Iraqi television lying in a hospital bed but not walking.
In Paris, a spokesman for the French foreign ministry confirmed a French medical team had examined Uday in Baghdad on what he called a private initiative.

The spokesman refused all comment on the opposition group's remarks, saying that the medical team's findings were in any case protected by medical confidentiality requirements. He declined to say whether French officials had been informed of the team's findings.
France said last Sunday that Uday would not be given medical treatment on its soil. A French foreign ministry spokesman did not give a reason for France's decision.

Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz told French television LCI that Baghdad was surprised but not angered by France's decision to refuse medical treatment to Uday. But Iraq's ruling Baath party newspaper Thawra said earlier that France would be committing a grave error if it stuck to its decision.
During a visit to France this week, Aziz praised Paris for breaking ranks with the United States and Britain in policing a no-fly zone in northern Iraq.
France was Iraq's main Western arms supplier before Iraq invaded Kuwait in 1990. Baghdad owes Paris more than $5 billion and the French are keen to restore economic ties once the embargo is lifted.
